lessons.title: Environmental and civic responsibility
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — Civic and social responsibility (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why the citizen must protect the environment and public property
Describe good practices for waste, water, trees and energy
Explain the role of the community and of the state
Link environment to sustainable development
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify health statements about water-related diseases and local environmental laws. The examples are general.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: The **environment** is everything around us: air, water, soil, plants, animals, buildings and people. Citizens depend on a healthy environment for food, water, health and livelihood, and have a duty to protect it for themselves and for **future generations**. **Sustainable development** means meeting today's needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

items.text: Also: sort waste, plant trees, save water

blocks.caption: Three ways to reduce waste
blocks.alt: Three circles labelled reduce, reuse and recycle.

blocks.title: Good practices
blocks.md:
- **Waste:** put rubbish in bins, sort it, reduce, reuse and recycle; never throw waste into gutters or rivers.
- **Water:** keep sources clean, do not waste water, treat or boil drinking water when needed.
- **Trees:** plant and protect trees; avoid bush fires.
- **Energy:** switch off unused lights, use clean energy where possible.
- **Public property:** schools, roads, lamps and water points belong to everyone and must be looked after.

**Community action:** clean-up days, tree-planting, neighbourhood drainage clearing, school environment clubs and awareness campaigns. **The state** makes environmental laws, creates protected areas, provides waste collection and water services and educates the public. Citizens help by following the law, reporting damage and taking part in community action.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- 'The government will clean it' is not enough: each person produces waste and must act responsibly.
- Blocked gutters cause floods; throwing plastic in them is dangerous, not harmless.
- Burning waste pollutes the air and is not a good way of getting rid of it.
- Sustainable development is not only about nature: it includes people's well-being and the economy.

blocks.title: Link with health
blocks.md: A dirty environment spreads diseases: poor waste disposal attracts rats and flies and blocks drains where mosquitoes breed; unsafe water causes cholera and typhoid. A clean environment protects health and saves money.

blocks.title: Example 1: practical action
blocks.statement: Name three things a school can do to keep its environment clean.
steps: Provide bins and teach pupils to use them.
Organise regular clean-up days and sort waste.
Plant trees and flowers and keep drains clear.
blocks.answer: Bins and sorting, clean-up days, trees and clear drains.

blocks.title: Example 2: cause and effect
blocks.statement: Explain how throwing plastic into a gutter can cause flooding.
steps: Plastic blocks the gutter and the flow of water.
During heavy rain water cannot drain and overflows.
Houses and roads are flooded.
blocks.answer: Blocked drains cause water to overflow during heavy rain.

lessons.title: Road safety
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — Civic and social responsibility (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why road safety matters
State the main causes of road accidents
Describe the rules for pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and drivers
State basic steps to take at an accident scene
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify against the current highway code and traffic law: sign shapes and colours, helmet and seat-belt rules, and the emergency telephone numbers (deliberately not given).

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: Road accidents injure and kill many people and cause great suffering and economic loss. Road safety is the responsibility of all road users: pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and drivers, as well as the authorities who build roads, set rules and enforce them. Most accidents are **caused by human behaviour** and can be prevented.

items.text: Green: go if the way is clear

blocks.caption: Traffic light colours
blocks.alt: A traffic light with red, yellow and green lamps and their meanings.

blocks.title: Main causes of accidents
blocks.md: **Speeding**; **drink-driving** and driving when tired; **using a phone** while driving; **overloading** vehicles and carrying too many passengers; **poor vehicle maintenance** (bad brakes and tyres); **ignoring signs, lights or the right of way**; **poor roads** and lack of lighting; and **bad weather** with unsuitable driving.

blocks.title: Safe behaviour
blocks.md:
- **Pedestrians:** use pavements, cross at crossings after looking right and left, stay alert and do not use phones while crossing; wear light-coloured clothes at night.
- **Motorcyclists and passengers:** wear a **helmet**, obey the rules, do not overload.
- **Drivers:** respect speed limits and signs, wear a **seat belt**, check the vehicle, never drive after drinking alcohol.
- **Everyone:** obey traffic lights and police signals.

**Road signs** are of three main kinds: **warning signs** (usually triangular), **regulatory or prohibitory signs** (usually round) and **information signs** (usually rectangular or square). Learn the meaning of common signs, such as stop, no entry, speed limit, pedestrian crossing and school ahead.

blocks.title: At an accident scene
blocks.md: Stay calm and make the area safe (warn other drivers); **call for help** from the emergency services; do not move seriously injured people unless there is immediate danger; give simple first aid if you are trained, such as stopping heavy bleeding; stay until help arrives. Check the emergency numbers with your teacher.

blocks.title: Example 1: identify the cause
blocks.statement: A bus overturns after taking too many passengers on a bad road at high speed. Identify two causes.
steps: Overloading makes the vehicle unstable.
High speed makes it hard to control on a poor road.
Both are human factors that could have been avoided.
blocks.answer: Overloading and speeding (plus a poor road).

blocks.title: Example 2: pedestrian rules
blocks.statement: Describe how to cross the road safely at a pedestrian crossing without lights.
steps: Stop at the edge and look right and left.
Wait until vehicles have stopped or there is a safe gap.
Cross quickly without running and keep watching traffic.
blocks.answer: Stop, look both ways, wait for a safe gap, then cross.

lessons.title: Health, hygiene and HIV/AIDS awareness
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — Civic and social responsibility (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain basic rules of personal and community hygiene
Define HIV and AIDS and describe how HIV is and is not transmitted
Describe ways of preventing HIV and caring for infected people
Explain why stigma must be fought
reviewNotes: IMPORTANT: Health content must be reviewed by a qualified health worker before release (transmission routes, prevention advice, ART statement, mother-to-child transmission wording and the hygiene list). Wording kept conservative and non-graphic.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: **Good health** means physical, mental and social well-being, not only the absence of disease. Good habits: **hand washing** with soap, safe drinking water, clean food and cooking, a balanced diet, clean surroundings, using mosquito nets to prevent malaria, exercise and rest, vaccination and going to a health centre when ill.

blocks.caption: How HIV is and is not passed on
blocks.alt: Two boxes listing how HIV can and cannot be passed on.

blocks.title: HIV and AIDS
blocks.md: **HIV** is the virus that weakens the body's immune system. **AIDS** is the advanced stage of HIV infection, when the body can no longer fight many illnesses. A person can have HIV for years without feeling ill, so only a **test** shows whether someone is infected. **Treatment** with antiretroviral medicines (ART) allows people with HIV to live long, healthy lives; it controls the virus but does not remove it.

blocks.title: Prevention
blocks.md:
- Do not have **unprotected sex**; abstinence, faithfulness to one tested partner and correct use of condoms reduce the risk.
- **Never share needles, razors or blades**; use sterile equipment.
- Use **safe blood** from approved centres.
- Pregnant women should be **tested**; treatment greatly reduces the risk of passing HIV to the baby.
- Get tested and seek advice from a health worker.

**Caring for people with HIV.** People with HIV can go to school, work and live normally; they can share meals and a home with family. They should follow medical advice and take their medication every day. Family and community support are very important.

blocks.title: Stigma and myths
blocks.md:
- HIV is **not** passed by hugging, shaking hands, sharing food or cups, toilets, coughing or mosquito bites.
- **Stigma** (shame and rejection) and discrimination prevent people from being tested and treated; they are unjust and harmful.
- Do not believe rumours or 'cures' sold by unqualified people. Always get information from a qualified health worker.

blocks.title: Example 1: true or false
blocks.statement: Is it safe to share a meal and a cup with a person who has HIV? Explain.
steps: HIV is not transmitted through food, cups or touching.
It passes through blood, sexual fluids and breast milk in specific ways.
So sharing meals is safe.

blocks.title: Example 2: prevention
blocks.statement: Give two ways in which a young person can protect themselves from HIV.
steps: Avoid unprotected sex (abstinence or condom use).
Never share needles, razors or blades.
Get advice and testing from a health worker.
blocks.answer: Avoid unprotected sex; never share needles or blades.

lessons.title: Corruption and good governance
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — Civic and social responsibility (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define corruption and name its forms
Explain its causes and effects
Describe ways of fighting corruption
Define good governance and its principles
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify definitions; no institutions, cases or political persons are named on purpose. Scenarios are hypothetical.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: **Corruption** is the misuse of a position, power or entrusted authority for private gain. It exists in many countries and in public and private institutions. Its harm is both material (lost money, poor services) and moral (loss of trust and fairness). Fighting corruption is a duty of every citizen.

items.text: All of them harm the common good

blocks.caption: Three forms of corruption
blocks.alt: Three boxes labelled bribery, embezzlement and favouritism, each with a short description.

blocks.title: Forms of corruption
blocks.md:
- **Bribery:** giving or taking money or gifts to obtain a favour or service.
- **Embezzlement:** stealing public money or goods entrusted to one's care.
- **Favouritism and nepotism:** giving jobs or advantages to relatives or friends unfairly.
- **Fraud and cheating:** for example in examinations, tenders or taxes.
- **Abuse of power or extortion:** demanding payments that are not due.

blocks.title: Causes and effects
blocks.md: **Causes:** greed, low salaries and poverty, weak controls, lack of transparency, impunity (no punishment), and a culture of tolerating small bribes. **Effects:** poor roads, schools and hospitals; wasted public funds; unfair competition; loss of trust in institutions; discouraging investors; and injustice for the poor.

**Fighting corruption:** clear laws and **punishment** for offenders; independent courts; audits and controls; **transparency** in public contracts and budgets; protection for people who report corruption; **education** in honesty; and **refusing to give or take bribes**. In school, copying in examinations and paying for marks are also forms of corruption.

blocks.title: Good governance
blocks.md: Good governance means managing public affairs in a way that serves the people. Its principles include **accountability** (leaders explain how they use power and money), **transparency** (information is open), **rule of law**, **participation** of citizens, **equity** (fair treatment), and **effectiveness**. Citizens help by voting responsibly, asking questions peacefully and taking part in community decisions.

blocks.title: Example 1: identify the form
blocks.statement: A clerk asks a citizen for extra money before processing an official paper that is free. Which form of corruption is this?
steps: The clerk uses their position to demand money.
This is a payment not due by law.
It is extortion, a form of corruption.

blocks.title: Example 2: effects
blocks.statement: Explain how corruption in the construction of a road can harm a community.
steps: Money meant for quality materials is stolen or wasted.
The road is built badly and breaks quickly.
The community suffers accidents, costs and delays.
blocks.answer: A poor-quality road, loss of public funds and danger for users.

lessons.title: International organisations and global citizenship
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — Civic and social responsibility (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why countries form international organisations
State the aims of the UN, the African Union, the Commonwealth and La Francophonie
Describe the role of regional groups and humanitarian organisations
Explain the idea of global citizenship
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify Cameroon's memberships (UN, AU, Commonwealth, La Francophonie, CEMAC), the agencies named and the description of the Commonwealth and CEMAC.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: No country can solve all problems alone. **International organisations** are groups of states (or of non-governmental bodies) that cooperate for common aims: peace, trade, health, education, human rights, development and protection of the environment. They give small and large countries a place to discuss and to act together.

items.text: Global, continental and linguistic or historical groupings

blocks.caption: Some international organisations
blocks.alt: A box UN at the top linked to boxes for the African Union, the Commonwealth and La Francophonie.

blocks.title: Main organisations
blocks.md:
- **United Nations (UN, 1945):** peace and security, human rights, development; its agencies include UNESCO, WHO, UNICEF and FAO.
- **African Union (AU):** unity, peace, security and development of Africa; it succeeded the OAU (1963) in 2002.
- **Commonwealth:** voluntary association of countries, mostly with a history linked to Britain, working together on democracy, education and trade.
- **La Francophonie:** organisation of countries sharing the French language and cultural ties.

**Regional economic groups** help neighbours to trade and cooperate: **CEMAC** (Central Africa; its members share the Central African CFA franc), **ECOWAS** (West Africa) and others. **Humanitarian organisations**, such as the **Red Cross and Red Crescent**, help victims of wars and disasters and are guided by humanity, neutrality and impartiality.

blocks.title: Cameroon and the world
blocks.md: Cameroon is a member of the UN, the African Union, the Commonwealth, La Francophonie and CEMAC. Membership brings cooperation in education, health, peacekeeping, trade and diplomacy, and also obligations, such as respecting international agreements and paying contributions.

blocks.title: Global citizenship
blocks.md: A **global citizen** is aware of the world, respects other cultures and human rights, and acts to solve shared problems such as poverty, climate change and conflict, while remaining loyal to their own country. Do not confuse these different organisations: each has its own membership and purpose.

blocks.title: Example 1: which organisation?
blocks.statement: Which organisation helps children and which one works for health?
steps: UNICEF works mainly for children's welfare.
WHO works for health.
Both are UN agencies.

blocks.title: Example 2: benefit of cooperation
blocks.statement: Give two benefits for Cameroon of regional cooperation in CEMAC.
steps: A common currency and market make trade easier.
Neighbouring states can share projects and infrastructure.
Cooperation can strengthen peace and development.
